proof:
**Step 1.** Choose the direct straight-production route. Suppose, for a contradiction, that a straight line ABC has its part AB in a plane Π, while its continuation BC rises out of Π. Here A, B, C occur in that order, and ABC is straight throughout, hence lies evenly with its points. [D1.4; supposition for contradiction.]

**Step 2.** In the plane Π, produce AB continuously in a straight line through B to D, taking the production BD longer than BC. This is straight production carried out in the given plane. [P2; D1.7.]

**Step 3.** BC and BD are both straight continuations of the same segment AB beyond B. They cannot diverge: a continuation departing from the straight course already fixed by the points of AB would no longer lie evenly with those points. Thus straight continuations cannot separate after a common segment, and BC coincides with the initial part of BD of its own length. [D1.4.]

**Step 4.** Since BD lies in Π, its coincident part BC also lies in Π, contrary to the supposition that BC rises out of Π. Therefore a part of a straight line cannot be in the plane of reference and another part in a plane more elevated. [Steps 1–3.]
statement: A part of a straight line cannot be in the plane of reference and a part in a plane more elevated.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the distinct straight lines ℓ and m cut one another at O, and choose a point Q on m different from O. Then Q is not on ℓ. Through Q draw a straight line n parallel to ℓ (1.31). This is the chosen route because the parallel construction supplies a common plane by the definition of parallel lines, rather than presupposing a plane containing ℓ and m.

**Step 2.** Since n and ℓ are parallel, they lie in one plane Π (D1.23). Thus O, which lies on ℓ, and Q, which lies on n, both belong to Π. Their straight join OQ lies in Π (P1, D1.7). This join is a nonzero segment of m.

**Step 3.** A straight line cannot have one part in a plane and another part elevated above it (11.1). Since the segment OQ of m lies in Π, the whole straight line m lies in Π. Therefore the two intersecting straight lines ℓ and m lie in one plane.

**Step 4.** Now let ABC be any triangle. Its side-lines AB and AC intersect at A, so the argument of Steps 1–3 places both in one plane Σ. In particular, B and C lie in Σ; hence their straight join BC also lies in Σ (P1, D1.7).

**Step 5.** All three sides AB, BC, and CA therefore lie in Σ, and the trilateral figure they bound—the triangle ABC—is in that plane (D1.19). Thus two intersecting straight lines are in one plane, and every triangle is in one plane.
statement: If two straight lines cut one another, they are in one plane, and every triangle is in one plane.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the distinct planes α and β cut one another, and let S be their common section. Choose distinct points A and B on S and join AB. The segment AB lies in each plane, since its endpoints lie in each plane (P1, D1.7). Produce AB to the straight line ℓ (P2). The whole line ℓ remains in both planes, since a straight line cannot lie partly in a plane and partly outside it (11.1).

**Step 2.** Suppose, for contradiction, that S contains a point C not on ℓ. Join AC and produce it to the straight line m. As in Step 1, m lies in both planes (P1, P2, D1.7, 11.1). Choose D on ℓ beyond B (P2). Thus B and D are distinct points of ℓ, neither lying on m.

**Step 3.** Since the planes are distinct, choose a point X in α but not in β, interchanging their names if necessary. Draw and produce the straight lines XB and XD; both lie in α (P1, P2, D1.7, 11.1). They are distinct: otherwise their common line would contain the segment BD in β, and 11.1 would force X also to lie in β.

**Step 4.** The line XB cannot meet m. For if it met m at E, then E and B would be distinct points of β. Consequently the segment BE would lie in β (D1.7), and the whole straight line XB would lie in β (11.1), contradicting the choice of X. The same reasoning, with D in place of B, shows that XD cannot meet m (D1.7, 11.1).

**Step 5.** Thus XB and XD are both parallel to m: they lie with m in α and do not meet it (D1.23). We now use 1.30 directly, since two lines parallel to the same line have arisen: it gives XB parallel to XD. But XB and XD meet at X, contrary to the definition of parallel straight lines (D1.23). This is the contradiction.

**Step 6.** Therefore S has no point outside ℓ. Conversely, the whole line ℓ belongs to both planes by Step 1 (11.1). Hence their common section S is exactly the straight line ℓ. Therefore, if two planes cut one another, their common section is a straight line.
statement: If two planes cut one another, their common section is a straight line.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the distinct straight lines a and b meet at O in the plane Π, and let p be perpendicular to both at O. The plane through a and b exists by 11.2. The line p cannot lie in Π: otherwise, choosing rays of a and b on opposite sides of p, their adjacent right angles with a ray of p would make those rays one straight line by 1.14, contradicting the distinctness of a and b. Moreover, p meets Π only at O; a second common point would put a segment of p in Π (D1.7), and hence the whole line there (11.1).

**Step 2.** Choose P on p, distinct from O, and produce PO through O to Q so that OQ = OP (P2, 1.3). Path choice: we shall use triangle congruence to obtain equal adjacent angles directly, rather than introduce squares of lengths.

**Step 3.** Let t be any straight line through O in Π. If t is a or b, its perpendicularity to p is given. Otherwise, choose a ray of t and points A on a and B on b on the two boundary rays of the sector containing it; join AB (P1). The chosen ray meets the interior of AB at a point T. Indeed, each base angle of triangle OAB together with angle AOB is less than two right angles (1.17). Each of the two angles into which the chosen ray divides angle AOB is smaller than the whole (CN5). Applying P5 with OA and then OB as transversal therefore gives the intersection on both ray AB and ray BA, so T lies between A and B.

**Step 4.** Join PA, QA, PB, QB, PT, and QT (P1). Every triangle used here is planar by 11.2. For X equal to A or B, the angles POX and QOX are right by the hypothesis and D1.10, and hence equal by P4. Since OP = OQ and OX is common, triangles POX and QOX are congruent by 1.4. Consequently PA = QA and PB = QB.

**Step 5.** Triangles PAB and QAB have PA = QA, PB = QB, and AB common. Therefore angle PAB equals angle QAB by 1.8. Since T lies between A and B, these are respectively angles PAT and QAT; thus angle PAT equals angle QAT.

**Step 6.** In triangles PAT and QAT, PA = QA, AT is common, and the included angles PAT and QAT are equal. Hence PT = QT by 1.4.

**Step 7.** Triangles POT and QOT now have OP = OQ, PT = QT, and OT common. Therefore angle POT equals angle QOT by 1.8. Since OP and OQ are opposite rays, these equal angles are adjacent angles on the straight line PQ. Each is consequently right by D1.10. Thus p is perpendicular to t.

**Step 8.** Every straight line in Π meeting p meets it at O, by Step 1, and every such line is perpendicular to p, by the hypothesis or Steps 3–7. Therefore p is at right angles to Π by D11.3, as required.
statement: If a straight line be set up at right angles to two straight lines which cut one another, at their common point of section, it will also be at right angles to the plane through them.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let OA, OB, and OC be the three given straight lines meeting at O, and let OD be perpendicular to each at O. The intersecting straight lines OA and OB lie in a plane Π. [Hypothesis; 11.2]

**Step 2.** Since OD is perpendicular to both OA and OB at their intersection, OD is perpendicular to Π. We use 11.4 directly to obtain perpendicularity to the plane, rather than reconstructing its proof. [11.4]

**Step 3.** Suppose, for a contradiction, that OC does not lie in Π. The intersecting lines OD and OC lie in a plane Σ, distinct from Π. These planes meet at O, and their common section is a straight line g through O. [11.2; 11.3]

**Step 4.** Since g lies in Π and passes through O, OD is perpendicular to g. Both g and OC lie in Σ. Choose a point E on g so that the ray OE lies on the opposite side of OD from the ray OC. Then ∠DOE is right, and ∠DOC is right by hypothesis. [D11.3; hypothesis]

**Step 5.** Thus, in Σ, the rays OE and OC lie on opposite sides of OD and make with it adjacent angles together equal to two right angles. Therefore OE and OC are in one straight line. Here 1.14 applies directly to the adjacent right angles, so no separate uniqueness theorem for perpendiculars is needed. [P4; 1.14]

**Step 6.** Consequently OC is part of the same straight line as g. Since g lies in Π, that straight line cannot have another part outside Π; hence OC also lies in Π, contrary to the supposition. Therefore OA, OB, and OC are all in one plane. [11.1]
statement: If a straight line be set up at right angles to three straight lines which meet one another, at their common point of section, the three straight lines are in one plane.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let l and m be distinct straight lines perpendicular to the same plane Π, meeting it at A and B respectively. Each therefore makes right angles with every straight line in Π through its foot [D11.3]. Our route is to establish coplanarity using 11.5 before applying a planar parallelism criterion.

**Step 2.** The feet A and B are distinct. For otherwise l and m would determine a plane [11.2], whose common section with Π would be a straight line s through their common foot [11.3]. Both l and m would be perpendicular to s [D11.3]. Choosing rays of l and m on opposite sides of s, their adjacent angles with a fixed ray of s would be two right angles; hence those rays would form one straight line [1.14]. This contradicts the distinctness of l and m.

**Step 3.** Join AB; it lies in Π [P1, D1.7]. In Π construct AC perpendicular to AB at A, with C distinct from A [1.11]. Choose a point X on m outside Π and not on l, and join AX, CX, and BC [P1]. Each triangle so formed lies in a plane [11.2].

**Step 4.** Triangle ABC is right-angled at A by construction. Since BA and BC lie in Π, triangles XBA and XBC are right-angled at B [D1.7, D11.3]. Consequently, writing YZ² for the square on YZ, the Pythagorean theorem gives
BC² = BA² + AC²,
XC² = XB² + BC²,
and XA² = XB² + BA² [1.47].

**Step 5.** Adding equal squares to the equalities in Step 4 and substituting gives
XC² = XB² + BA² + AC² = XA² + AC² [CN2, CN1].
Therefore the angle XAC is right, by the converse of the Pythagorean theorem [1.48]. This supplies the additional perpendicular needed for the coplanarity argument.

**Step 6.** At A, the straight line AC is perpendicular to AB by construction, to l because AC lies in Π [D11.3], and to AX by Step 5. Thus the three straight lines AB, l, and AX lie in one plane, say Q [11.5].

**Step 7.** Both B and X belong to Q. Their joining segment BX therefore lies in Q [D1.7], and its whole supporting straight line m lies in Q [11.1]. Hence l and m are coplanar.

**Step 8.** In Q, the transversal AB makes right angles with both l and m [D11.3]. Its interior angles on the same side therefore sum to two right angles, so l and m are parallel [1.28]. This is the direct planar criterion because the two interior right angles are already available. Thus two distinct straight lines perpendicular to the same plane are parallel.
statement: If two straight lines be at right angles to the same plane, the straight lines will be parallel.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let l and m be the given parallel straight lines, and take arbitrary points A on l and B on m. By the definition of parallel straight lines, l and m lie in a plane Π and do not meet; in particular, B is not on l. [D1.23]

**Step 2.** Join A to B. [P1] The distinct straight lines l and AB meet at A, so they lie in a plane Σ. [11.2] Path choice: use the intersecting-lines clause of 11.2 directly, since these lines already meet; no auxiliary triangle is needed.

**Step 3.** Suppose Σ and Π were distinct. Since both contain l, they intersect, and their common section is a straight line. [11.3] This common section contains l and therefore is l itself. But B belongs to Π because it lies on m, and belongs to Σ because it lies on AB. Thus B would lie on the common section l, contradicting the fact that the parallel lines l and m do not meet. [D1.23] Therefore Σ and Π are the same plane.

**Step 4.** The joining straight line AB lies in Σ by Step 2, and hence in Π by Step 3. Since Π also contains both parallel straight lines, AB is in the same plane with them, as required. [11.2, D1.23]
statement: If two straight lines be parallel and points be taken at random on each of them, the straight line joining the points is in the same plane with the parallel straight lines.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let l and m be parallel straight lines, and let l be perpendicular to the plane Π at A. The parallel lines lie in a common plane Σ [D1.23]. This plane is distinct from Π because it contains l; their common section is therefore a straight line t through A [11.3]. Since t lies in Π, l is perpendicular to t [D11.3].

**Step 2.** The line m meets t. For otherwise m would be parallel to t in Σ [D1.23]; since l is also parallel to m, l would be parallel to t [1.30], contradicting their meeting at A. Let B be the intersection of m and t. Then B differs from A [D1.23], and m is perpendicular to t by the equality of corresponding angles made by a transversal with parallel lines [1.29]. Moreover, m is not contained in Π: otherwise it would lie in the common section t, contrary to its being perpendicular to t [11.3].

**Step 3.** In Π draw s through B perpendicular to t [1.11]. Since m is not contained in Π, m and s are distinct intersecting lines; let Λ be a plane containing them [11.2]. The line t is perpendicular to both m and s at B, so t is perpendicular to Λ [11.4].

**Step 4.** In Λ draw n through B perpendicular to s [1.11]. Because t is perpendicular to Λ and n lies in Λ through B, t is perpendicular to n [D11.3]. Thus n is perpendicular to both s and t at their intersection B. Since s and t lie in Π, n is perpendicular to Π [11.4]. This is the chosen two-line route: use 11.4 to obtain a normal at B, rather than verify perpendicularity to every line of Π separately.

**Step 5.** Now l and n are perpendicular to the same plane Π, so the directly applicable proposition 11.6 gives l parallel to n [11.6]. Let Ω be their common plane [D1.23]. Both Ω and Σ contain the entire line l and also the point B, which is not on l. Consequently Ω and Σ coincide: if they were distinct, their common section would be a single straight line, which could not contain both l and a point outside l [11.3]. Hence n and m both lie in Σ.

**Step 6.** If n and m were distinct, then, being in Σ and both parallel to l, they would be parallel to one another [1.30]. But they meet at B, contrary to the definition of parallel lines [D1.23]. Therefore n and m coincide. Since n is perpendicular to Π by Step 4, m is perpendicular to Π, as required.
statement: If two straight lines be parallel, and one of them be at right angles to any plane, the remaining one will also be at right angles to the same plane.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let a and b each be parallel to c, and suppose that no single plane contains all three lines. By the definition of parallel straight lines, a and c lie in a plane α, while b and c lie in a plane β. These planes are distinct by hypothesis. Choose a point O on c. [D1.23]

**Step 2.** In α draw a straight line x through O perpendicular to c, and in β draw a straight line y through O perpendicular to c. [1.11] The common section of α and β is c. Hence x and y are distinct: if they coincided, their common line would lie in that section and thus coincide with c, contrary to their construction as perpendiculars to c. [11.3]

**Step 3.** Since x and y intersect at O, they lie in a plane σ. [11.2] The line c is perpendicular to both x and y at their common point O; therefore c is perpendicular to σ. [11.4]

**Step 4.** Since a is parallel to c and c is perpendicular to σ, a is also perpendicular to σ. Likewise, since b is parallel to c, b is perpendicular to σ. [11.8]

**Step 5.** The straight lines a and b are perpendicular to the same plane σ; therefore they are parallel to one another. [11.6] This is the natural concluding criterion: the common perpendicular plane allows 11.6 to establish parallelism without first assuming that a and b are coplanar. Thus the required proposition is proved.
statement: Straight lines which are parallel to the same straight line and are not in the same plane with it are also parallel to one another.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the first pair of straight lines meet at A and the second pair at D, and denote them by AB, AC and DE, DF respectively, where AB ∥ DE and AC ∥ DF. Each intersecting pair lies in a plane by 11.2; by hypothesis, the four lines do not all lie in one plane.

**Step 2.** Join AD (P1). By 11.7, AD lies both in the plane of the parallels AB, DE and in the plane of the parallels AC, DF. Choose B and E on the same side of AD in the first of these planes, and C and F on the same side of AD in the second. Thus the chosen rays represent corresponding directions. Shortening the longer of each pair of segments when necessary, arrange that AB = DE and AC = DF (1.3).

**Step 3.** Join BE, CF, BC, and EF (P1). By 11.7, BE lies in the plane of AB and DE, and CF lies in the plane of AC and DF. Apply 1.33 to the equal parallel segments AB and DE, whose corresponding endpoints are A, D and B, E: it gives AD ∥ BE and AD = BE. Applying 1.33 likewise to AC and DF gives AD ∥ CF and AD = CF. This is the direct path: 1.33 supplies both the parallelism and the equality of the joining segments at once.

**Step 4.** The three lines AD, BE, and CF cannot all lie in one plane. Otherwise, by 11.7, their joining lines AB, DE, AC, and DF would all lie in that plane, contrary to the hypothesis. Since BE and CF are parallel to AD and are not all coplanar with it, BE ∥ CF by 11.9. Moreover, BE = CF, since each equals AD (CN1).

**Step 5.** The endpoint correspondences established in Step 3 are A with D, B with E, and C with F. Hence BC and EF join the equal parallel segments BE and CF at corresponding ends. Applying 1.33 again gives BC = EF.

**Step 6.** The triangles ABC and DEF are each planar by 11.2. Their corresponding sides satisfy AB = DE and AC = DF by Step 2, and BC = EF by Step 5. Therefore their angles contained by the first two pairs of equal sides are equal by 1.8: ∠BAC = ∠EDF. Thus the two pairs of intersecting straight lines contain equal corresponding angles, as required.
statement: If two straight lines meeting one another be parallel to two straight lines meeting one another not in the same plane, they will contain equal angles.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given point outside the given plane Π. Take a straight line ℓ in Π and a point B on ℓ. Join AB [P1]. The intersecting lines AB and ℓ lie in one plane, which we call Σ [11.2].

**Step 2.** In Σ draw AD perpendicular to ℓ, with D on ℓ [1.12]. In Π draw the straight line m through D perpendicular to ℓ [1.11]. Since A is outside Π, AD and m are distinct; being intersecting straight lines, they lie in a plane Q [11.2].

**Step 3.** The line ℓ is perpendicular to both AD and m at their common point D. Therefore ℓ is perpendicular to their plane Q [11.4].

**Step 4.** Since A is outside Π and m lies in Π, A is not on m. In Q draw AF perpendicular to m, with F on m [1.12]. Thus F belongs to Π. We shall show that AF is the required perpendicular.

**Step 5.** If F=D, let n be ℓ; then n lies in Π and is perpendicular to Q by Step 3. If F≠D, draw through F in Π the line n parallel to ℓ [1.31]. Since ℓ is perpendicular to Q, n is also perpendicular to Q [11.8]. This uses the direct perpendicularity-transfer theorem rather than a separate comparison of angles. In either case, m and n are distinct: in the first case they are perpendicular by Step 2; in the second, m meets ℓ whereas n, being parallel to ℓ, does not [D1.23].

**Step 6.** The line AF lies in Q and meets n at F. Since n is perpendicular to Q, it makes right angles with AF [D11.3]. Also AF is perpendicular to m by Step 4. Hence AF is perpendicular to the two distinct lines m and n at their common point F, and therefore is perpendicular to their plane Π [11.4]. Thus from the given elevated point A we have drawn AF perpendicular to the given plane Π, as required.
statement: From a given elevated point to draw a straight line perpendicular to a given plane.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let Π be the given plane and A the given point in it. Choose a point B outside Π. From B draw BC perpendicular to Π, meeting Π at C. [11.11]

**Step 2.** If A lies on BC, then BC itself is the required straight line through A, since it is perpendicular to Π. [11.11] Otherwise, join AB. [P1] The intersecting straight lines AB and BC lie in one plane Σ, which therefore contains A and BC. [11.2]

**Step 3.** In Σ, draw through A a straight line AD parallel to BC. [1.31] The chosen route is to transfer the known perpendicularity by this parallel construction, rather than establish individual right angles afresh.

**Step 4.** Since BC is perpendicular to Π and AD is parallel to BC, AD is also perpendicular to Π. [11.8] Thus AD is a straight line set up at right angles to the given plane from the given point A in it, as required.
statement: To set up a straight line at right angles to a given plane from a given point in it.

proof:
**Step 1.** Suppose, for contradiction, that two distinct rays OA and OB are set up from the same point O perpendicular to the same plane Π and on the same side of it. Their supporting straight lines are distinct: otherwise the rays would either coincide or lie on opposite sides of Π. Since both straight lines are perpendicular to Π, they are parallel by **11.6**. This is the direct path: apply the established parallelism theorem without constructing an auxiliary plane.

**Step 2.** By **D1.23**, parallel straight lines do not meet, even when produced indefinitely. But the supporting lines of OA and OB both contain O, a contradiction. Therefore, from the same point two distinct straight lines cannot be set up at right angles to the same plane on the same side.
statement: From the same point two straight lines cannot be set up at right angles to the same plane on the same side.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let Π and Σ be distinct planes, and let the straight line l be perpendicular to both, meeting them at A and B respectively. A perpendicular is not contained in the plane to which it is perpendicular (D11.3); consequently, by 11.1, l meets each plane only at its respective foot.

**Step 2.** The feet A and B are distinct. For otherwise, let their common point be O. Choose two intersecting straight lines r and s through O in Π, and a straight line t through O in Σ not contained in Π; such a choice is possible because the planes are distinct (P1, 11.1, 11.3). By D11.3, l is perpendicular to all three lines. Therefore r, s, and t lie in one plane by 11.5. That plane must be Π: otherwise its common section with Π would contain the two intersecting lines r and s, contrary to 11.3. This would put t in Π, a contradiction. Hence A ≠ B.

**Step 3.** Suppose that Π and Σ meet, and take a common point C. By Steps 1–2, C cannot lie on l. Join AC and BC (P1). Since their endpoints belong to the respective planes, AC lies in Π and BC lies in Σ (11.1).

**Step 4.** The noncollinear points A, B, and C form a triangle lying in one plane (11.2). Since AB lies on the common perpendicular l, while AC lies in Π and BC lies in Σ, both ∠CAB and ∠ABC are right angles (D11.3).

**Step 5.** But any two angles of a triangle are together less than two right angles (1.17), whereas these two angles are themselves two right angles. This is a contradiction. The direct two-angle bound of 1.17 is the natural choice here; no calculation of the full triangle-angle sum is needed.

**Step 6.** Thus Π and Σ do not meet. Planes which do not meet are parallel (D11.8). Therefore planes to which the same straight line is at right angles are parallel.
statement: Planes to which the same straight line is at right angles will be parallel.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight lines a and b meet at A, and let c and d meet at B, with a parallel to c and b parallel to d. Let Π and Σ be their respective planes, which exist by 11.2 and are distinct by hypothesis. We choose the common-perpendicular route: we shall exhibit a straight line perpendicular to both planes and apply 11.14.

**Step 2.** The point B is outside Π. For suppose B belonged to Π. Since c is parallel to a and d is parallel to b, B lies on neither a nor b [D1.23]. The plane containing the parallel lines a and c would then share with Π both the line a and the point B outside a. These planes must coincide, since otherwise their common section would be a single straight line [11.3]. Thus c lies in Π; the same argument shows that d lies in Π. Consequently Π and Σ would contain both intersecting lines c and d and would therefore coincide, again by 11.3. This contradicts the hypothesis.

**Step 3.** Draw BH perpendicular to Π, with H in Π [11.11]. Thus BH makes right angles with every straight line in Π passing through H [D11.3].

**Step 4.** If H lies on a, take r to be a itself; otherwise, through H draw r in Π parallel to a. Similarly, take s to be b itself if H lies on b, and otherwise draw s through H in Π parallel to b [1.31].

**Step 5.** We have r parallel to c. This is the hypothesis if r equals a. Otherwise r and a are distinct parallel lines in Π, whereas c contains B outside Π; hence these three lines are not coplanar. Since r and c are both parallel to a, the spatial parallel-transitivity theorem 11.9 applies and gives r parallel to c. The identical argument gives s parallel to d [11.9].

**Step 6.** Since H and B lie respectively on the parallel lines r and c, the joining straight line BH lies in their plane [11.7]. Its angles with r at H are right angles [D11.3]; therefore its angles with c at B are also right angles [1.29]. Applying the same argument to the parallel lines s and d shows that BH also makes right angles with d at B [11.7, D11.3, 1.29].

**Step 7.** Thus BH is at right angles to both c and d at their common point B. It is therefore perpendicular to their plane Σ [11.4].

**Step 8.** The same straight line BH is perpendicular to Π by construction and to Σ by Step 7. Hence Π and Σ are parallel [11.14], as required.
statement: If two straight lines meeting one another be parallel to two straight lines meeting one another, not being in the same plane, the planes through them are parallel.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the parallel planes α and β be cut by a plane γ, and denote their common sections with γ by ℓ and m, respectively. By 11.3, ℓ and m are straight lines; both lie in γ.

**Step 2.** By 11.1, the straight line ℓ remains in α and γ however far it is produced in either direction. Likewise, m remains in β and γ however far it is produced in either direction.

**Step 3.** If ℓ and m met at any point P, including upon production, Step 2 would place P in both α and β. Those planes would therefore meet, contrary to their being parallel (D11.8). Hence ℓ and m do not meet in either direction.

**Step 4.** The straight lines ℓ and m lie in the same plane γ and, when produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet. Therefore they are parallel by D1.23. This direct defining criterion is the natural route, since coplanarity and non-intersection have already been established. Thus the common sections of the two parallel planes with the cutting plane are parallel.
statement: If two parallel planes be cut by any plane, their common sections are parallel.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let α, β, γ be three parallel planes, with β between α and γ. These planes do not meet one another [D11.8]. Let them cut the first straight line at A, B, C, respectively, and the second at D, E, F, respectively. Thus B lies between A and C, and E between D and F. We must prove AB:BC = DE:EF.

**Step 2.** First suppose that A ≠ D and C ≠ F. Join AF, AD, and CF [P1]. The triangles ACF and ADF each lie in a plane [11.2]. Let AF meet the middle plane β at X, between A and F. The chosen route is to obtain parallel sections in these two triangle planes and then use proportional division directly, rather than establish similarity.

**Step 3.** In the plane of triangle ACF, the sections with β and γ are the straight lines BX and CF [11.3]. Since β and γ are parallel, BX ∥ CF [11.16]. Similarly, in the plane of triangle ADF, the sections with α and β are AD and EX [11.3]; hence AD ∥ EX [11.16].

**Step 4.** In triangle ACF, since BX is parallel to CF, proportional division gives
AB:BC = AX:XF [6.2].
In triangle FDA, since EX is parallel to DA, proportional division gives
FE:ED = FX:XA [6.2].
Reversing both ratios gives DE:EF = AX:XF. Such reversal preserves equality of ratios because the defining comparisons of equimultiples are reversed together [D5.5].

**Step 5.** The ratios AB:BC and DE:EF are therefore each equal to AX:XF. Consequently,
AB:BC = DE:EF [5.11].

**Step 6.** The cases of a common outer intersection require only one triangle. If A = D, form triangle ACF [P1, 11.2]. Its middle-plane section BE is parallel to CF [11.3, 11.16], so AB:BC = AE:EF = DE:EF [6.2]. If C = F, form triangle CAD [P1, 11.2]. Its middle-plane section BE is parallel to AD [11.3, 11.16], so CB:BA = CE:ED [6.2]; reversing both ratios gives AB:BC = ED:CE = DE:EF [D5.5]. If the two straight lines coincide, their corresponding segments coincide, and the required ratios are identical [D5.5]. Thus in every case the corresponding intercepted segments are proportional. Since the three parallel planes were arbitrary, two straight lines cut by parallel planes are cut in the same ratios.
statement: If two straight lines be cut by parallel planes, they will be cut in the same ratios.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line l be perpendicular to the plane α at O, and let β be any plane containing l. The common section of α and β is a straight line s through O (11.3). We take the direct route of verifying that every straight line in β perpendicular to s is perpendicular to α, as required by D11.4.

**Step 2.** Since s lies in α and meets l at O, the given perpendicularity of l to α implies that l is perpendicular to s (D11.3).

**Step 3.** Let X be any point of s different from O, and let m be any straight line in β through X perpendicular to s. The lines l and m are coplanar, and the transversal s makes equal corresponding right angles with them (P4). Hence m is parallel to l (1.28). This parallelism criterion applies directly because the corresponding angles are right angles. Since l is perpendicular to α, its parallel m is also perpendicular to α (11.8).

**Step 4.** At O, any straight line m in β perpendicular to s must coincide with l. Indeed, choose a ray of m and a ray of l on opposite sides of s. With a fixed ray of s from O, they make adjacent angles whose sum is two right angles. Therefore those two rays lie in a straight line, so m and l coincide (1.14). Consequently m is perpendicular to α by the hypothesis on l.

**Step 5.** Thus every straight line drawn in β at right angles to the common section s is perpendicular to α. Therefore β is at right angles to α (D11.4). Since β was an arbitrary plane through l, all planes through l are at right angles to α, as required.
statement: If a straight line be at right angles to any plane, all the planes through it will also be at right angles to the same plane.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the distinct planes α and β cut one another, and let each be at right angles to the plane π. Denote their common section by ℓ, and their respective common sections with π by a and b. The sections a and b exist by the hypothesis of perpendicular planes (D11.4), and all three common sections are straight lines (11.3).

**Step 2.** Choose a point X on ℓ. In α draw a straight line m through X perpendicular to a: use 1.11 if X lies on a, and 1.12 otherwise. Likewise, in β draw a straight line n through X perpendicular to b, using 1.11 if X lies on b and 1.12 otherwise. Thus m lies in α and n lies in β, and both pass through X (1.11, 1.12).

**Step 3.** Since α is perpendicular to π, the line m, drawn in α perpendicular to their common section a, is perpendicular to π. Likewise, since β is perpendicular to π, the line n is perpendicular to π (D11.4).

**Step 4.** If m and n were distinct, they would be parallel, since both are perpendicular to the same plane π (11.6). But both pass through X, whereas parallel straight lines do not meet (D1.23). Therefore m and n are the same straight line. This parallelism criterion is the direct choice here because it does not require X to lie in π.

**Step 5.** This coincident line lies in both α and β, so it is their common straight-line section ℓ (11.3). Since it is perpendicular to π by Step 3 (D11.4), ℓ is perpendicular to π. Therefore the common section of the two given planes is at right angles to the same plane, as required.
statement: If two planes which cut one another be at right angles to any plane, their common section will also be at right angles to the same plane.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the solid angle have vertex O and three noncoplanar edges in the directions OA, OB, OC. Write α = ∠AOB, β = ∠AOC, and γ = ∠BOC; take α as an arbitrary one of the three plane angles (D11.11). We shall prove β + γ > α. If β ≥ α, then β + γ > β ≥ α, since the whole is greater than its part (CN5). Thus it remains to consider α > β. Our chosen construction copies β inside α.

**Step 2.** Choose points A and B on the first two edges and join AB (P1). The intersecting lines OA and OB lie in one plane (11.2). In that plane construct a ray OD inside ∠AOB such that ∠AOD = β (1.23). Since 0 < β < α, this ray meets AB at a point D strictly between A and B.

**Step 3.** On the third edge choose C such that OC = OD, producing the edge first if necessary (P2, 1.3). Join AC and BC (P1). The noncoplanarity of the three edges ensures that A, B, C are not collinear; thus ABC is a nondegenerate triangle, and it lies in one plane (D11.11, 11.2).

**Step 4.** In triangles OAD and OAC, OA is common, OD = OC, and ∠AOD = ∠AOC by construction. Therefore their bases are equal: AD = AC (1.4).

**Step 5.** In triangle ABC, AC + BC > AB (1.20). Since D lies between A and B, AB = AD + DB. Substituting AC = AD and subtracting the equal lengths gives BC > DB (CN3).

**Step 6.** Compare triangles BOC and BOD. They have BO common and OC = OD, while their third sides satisfy BC > BD. Consequently ∠BOC > ∠BOD (1.25). This proposition applies directly because the comparison of the third sides has already been established.

**Step 7.** Add ∠AOC = ∠AOD to this strict inequality. Since OD lies inside ∠AOB, it follows that
∠AOC + ∠BOC > ∠AOD + ∠DOB = ∠AOB
(CN2, CN5). Thus β + γ > α. Because α was an arbitrary one of the three plane angles, any two of them, taken together in any manner, are greater than the remaining one.
statement: If a solid angle be contained by three plane angles, any two, taken together in any manner, are greater than the remaining one.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let S be the vertex of the given solid angle. Cut off its convex corner by a plane not through S, meeting its edge-rays, in cyclic order, at A₁, …, Aₙ, where n ≥ 3. The section is a convex polygon: its sides are the straight intersections of the cutting plane with the successive face-planes. The cut-off solid is a pyramid, and its lateral triangles SAᵢAᵢ₊₁ contain at S precisely the plane angles in question. Indices are understood cyclically. We use this section so that the direct comparison in 11.20 applies at every base vertex, treating all numbers of faces together. [D11.11, D11.12, 11.3]

**Step 2.** Let R denote a right angle, and let βᵢ = ∠Aᵢ₋₁AᵢAᵢ₊₁ be the interior angle of the section at Aᵢ. Draw the diagonals from A₁ to its nonadjacent vertices. They divide the convex section into n − 2 triangles, whose angles together constitute exactly the interior angles of the polygon. Applying the triangle-angle sum and adding gives
B := ∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ βᵢ = 2(n − 2)R.
This uses 1.32 directly because the section has been divided into triangles. [P1, 1.32, CN2]

**Step 3.** At each Aᵢ, the three rays AᵢAᵢ₋₁, AᵢS, and AᵢAᵢ₊₁ form a solid angle contained by three plane angles: the two base rays are noncollinear in the section plane, whereas S is outside that plane. Hence 11.20 gives
∠Aᵢ₋₁AᵢS + ∠SAᵢAᵢ₊₁ > βᵢ.
Let T be the sum of the expressions on the left over all i. Adding these strict inequalities yields T > B; thus T = B + E for some positive angular excess E. [D11.11, 11.20, CN2, CN5]

**Step 4.** Put F := ∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ ∠AᵢSAᵢ₊₁, the sum of the plane angles containing the original solid angle. The n lateral triangles have total angle sum 2nR. Their angles at S sum to F, while their remaining angles sum to T, each occurring exactly once. Therefore
F + T = 2nR.
[1.32, CN2]

**Step 5.** Substitute T = B + E and B = 2(n − 2)R into the preceding equality. It follows that
F + 2(n − 2)R + E = 2nR.
Subtracting the common magnitude 2(n − 2)R gives F + E = 4R. Since E is positive, F is a proper part of four right angles and therefore F < 4R. Thus any solid angle is contained by plane angles whose sum is less than four right angles. [CN1, CN3, CN5]
statement: Any solid angle is contained by plane angles less than four right angles.

proof:
**Step 1.** Denote the three given angles by α, β, γ, relabelled so that γ ≥ α ≥ β. Let r be the common length of all their containing straight lines, and let a, b, c respectively be the straight lines joining their extremities, drawn by P1. By hypothesis, α + β > γ.

**Step 2.** Comparing the triangles containing the given angles gives c ≥ a ≥ b: unequal angles give the corresponding strict inequalities by 1.24, while equal angles give equal opposite sides by 1.4. This is the direct comparison because the two containing sides of every angle are already equal. Our route is to verify the side inequalities and then apply 1.22; since c is greatest, only a + b > c requires proof.

**Step 3.** If γ = α, then c = a by 1.4, and therefore a + b > c by CN5. For the remaining case, suppose γ > α.

**Step 4.** Let AOB be the given angle γ, so that OA = OB = r and AB = c. Describe the circle with centre O and radius r; it passes through A and B (P3; D1.15). Within angle AOB construct a ray making angle α with OA, and let C be its intersection with the circle (1.23). Thus ∠AOC = α and OC = r; since 0 < α < γ, the points A, B, C are distinct. Join AC and BC (D1.15; P1).

**Step 5.** The remaining angle satisfies ∠COB = γ − α < β, by α + β > γ and removal of the common angle α (CN3; CN5). Comparing triangle AOC with the given triangle containing α gives AC = a by 1.4. Comparing triangle BOC with the given triangle containing β gives BC < b by 1.24, since their corresponding containing sides are all equal to r.

**Step 6.** The points A, B, C are noncollinear: otherwise the middle one would lie inside the circle by 3.2 applied to the outer two, although it lies on the circumference. Hence 1.20 applies to triangle ABC and gives AB < AC + BC. Together with Step 5, this yields c = AB < AC + BC < a + b. Thus a + b > c also in the case γ > α (1.20; CN5).

**Step 7.** In both cases, a + b > c. Since c ≥ a ≥ b and every given joining segment is positive, c + b > a and c + a > b as well (CN5). Therefore any two of a, b, c together exceed the remaining one. By 1.22, a triangle can be constructed with sides equal to a, b, c—that is, out of the straight lines joining the extremities of the given equal straight lines. This proves the proposition.
statement: If there be three plane angles of which two, taken together in any manner, are greater than the remaining one, and they are contained by equal straight lines, it is possible to construct a triangle out of the straight lines joining the extremities of the equal straight lines.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the given angles be α, β, γ, and let R denote a right angle. Assume that each pair exceeds the remaining angle and that α + β + γ < 4R. The latter is the necessary proviso stated in the proposition, since every solid angle has its containing plane angles together less than four right angles (11.21). Subtraction gives
|α − β| < γ < min(α + β, 4R − α − β).
(CN3.) We choose a planar-chord construction followed by a perpendicular lift; this avoids cases concerning the position of a circumcentre.

**Step 2.** In a plane Π describe a circle Γ with centre O and radius r. Choose points A, B, C on Γ so that ∠AOB = α and ∠AOC = β, with B and C on the same side of OA (P3, 1.23, D1.15). Reflect C across the line OA: draw CH perpendicular to OA, and produce CH to D so that HD = HC (1.12, P2, 1.3). The right triangles OHC and OHD show that OD = OC = r and ∠AOD = β; when H = O these conclusions are immediate. Thus D belongs to Γ and lies on the opposite side of OA from C (1.4, P4, 1.13). In particular, CD is perpendicular to OA.

**Step 3.** Choose X on Γ so that ∠BOX = γ, and join the required points (1.23, P1). Put a = BX. The smaller angle between OB and OC is |α − β|, while that between OB and OD is δ = min(α + β, 4R − α − β) (1.13). Therefore Step 1 and the comparison of triangles with two equal sides give
BC < a < BD.
(1.24.) The boundary configurations require no exception to this conclusion: if B = C, the first inequality is immediate; if δ = 2R, then BD = 2r and BX < BO + OX = 2r by 1.20.

**Step 4.** We use the following projection form of 2.12 and 2.13. For a fixed segment OP = r and a point Z in Π, let u(Z) be the directed distance from O to the perpendicular projection of Z on the line OP, positive towards P. Then
PZ² − OZ² = r² − 2r·u(Z).
Here squares and products denote square and rectangular areas, with a negative directed product recording subtraction. This identity is precisely the obtuse- and acute-angle square relations of 2.12 and 2.13; the right-angle and collinear configurations follow from 1.47 and 2.4, respectively (CN2, CN3).

**Step 5.** Drop XK perpendicular to OB, and draw through K the line ℓ perpendicular to OB (1.12, 1.11). Apply Step 4 with P = B. Since OC = OX = OD = r, the inequalities BC < BX < BD imply
u(C) > u(X) > u(D),
where the projections are now taken on OB. Thus the projections of C and D lie strictly on opposite sides of K. Consequently ℓ meets the segment CD in an interior point T: the perpendicular projection lines are parallel, and their order on OB gives this interior intersection by the parallel-line angle relations and P5 (1.29, P4). Since T lies on ℓ, u(T) = u(X).

**Step 6.** The point T is strictly inside the chord CD, and hence inside Γ (3.2). Therefore OT < r (CN5). This strict inequality is what will give the constructed vertex a positive height above Π.

**Step 7.** Because CD is perpendicular to OA, T and C have the same perpendicular projection on OA. Applying Step 4 first with P = A, and then with P = B, gives
AT² − OT² = AC² − OC² = AC² − r²,
BT² − OT² = BX² − OX² = a² − r².
The second equality uses the common projection of T and X established in Step 5; the radii equalities follow from D1.15.

**Step 8.** Construct squares on r and OT, and construct a square equal to their positive difference; let its side be h. Thus h² = r² − OT² and h > 0 (1.46, 2.14, Step 6). At T erect a perpendicular to Π and mark S on it with TS = h (11.12, P2, 1.3). By D11.3 and 1.47,
OS² = OT² + TS² = r².
If T = O, the same conclusion is immediate from OS = TS = h = r. Hence OS = r; equality of square areas entails equality of their sides by 2.4 and CN5.

**Step 9.** The triangles ATS and BTS are right-angled at T (D11.3). Therefore Step 7 and 1.47 give
AS² = AT² + TS² = AT² + r² − OT² = AC²,
BS² = BT² + TS² = BT² + r² − OT² = a².
(CN2, CN3.) Consequently AS = AC and BS = BX, again by 2.4 and CN5.

**Step 10.** Compare triangles AOS and AOC. Their three corresponding sides are equal: AO is common, OS = OC = r, and AS = AC. Hence ∠AOS = ∠AOC = β (1.8). Likewise, triangles BOS and BOX have BO common, OS = OX = r, and BS = BX; hence ∠BOS = ∠BOX = γ (1.8). The remaining angle ∠AOB is α by construction. The side-side-side proposition 1.8 is the natural comparison here because all three corresponding sides have already been established equal. Finally, TS > 0 and TS is perpendicular to Π, so S is outside Π. Since OA and OB are distinct intersecting lines in Π, the three rays OA, OB, OS cannot lie in one plane (11.3). They therefore contain a solid angle whose three plane angles are exactly α, β, γ (D11.11). The required solid angle has been constructed.
statement: To construct a solid angle out of three plane angles two of which, taken together in any manner, are greater than the remaining one: thus the three angles must be less than four right angles.

proof:
**Step 1.** Choose an arbitrary pair of opposite faces of the solid and name them ABCD and EFGH, with corresponding vertices A, E; B, F; C, G; and D, H. The other opposite pairs are ABFE and DCGH, and ADHE and BCGF. By hypothesis, the planes of each opposite pair are parallel. Their common sections, which form the edges, are straight lines [11.3].

**Step 2.** The plane ABCD cuts the parallel planes ABFE and DCGH in AB and DC; therefore AB is parallel to DC. It also cuts the parallel planes ADHE and BCGF in AD and BC; therefore AD is parallel to BC [11.16]. Thus ABCD is a parallelogram. The same argument applies to every face: each cuts the other two pairs of parallel bounding planes, so both pairs of its opposite sides are parallel [11.16]. Hence all six faces are parallelograms.

**Step 3.** In the parallelogram ABFE, opposite sides AB and EF are equal; in the parallelogram ADHE, opposite sides AD and EH are equal [1.34]. Consequently, AB = EF and AD = EH. Moreover, AB is parallel to EF, and AD is parallel to EH, by Step 2.

**Step 4.** The intersecting straight lines AB and AD are respectively parallel, in corresponding directions, to the intersecting straight lines EF and EH in the other plane. Therefore angle BAD equals angle FEH [11.10]. This supplies the included-angle equality directly from the parallel sides.

**Step 5.** Join BD and FH in their respective faces [P1]. The triangles BAD and FEH have BA = FE, AD = EH, and the included angle BAD equal to the included angle FEH. Therefore these triangles are equal [1.4]. Side–angle–side is the direct choice here because precisely these two side equalities and their included-angle equality have already been established.

**Step 6.** The diagonal BD bisects the parallelogram ABCD, and the diagonal FH bisects the parallelogram EFGH [1.34]. Thus ABCD and EFGH are respectively doubles of the equal triangles BAD and FEH, and are therefore equal [CN2]. Since the opposite pair was chosen arbitrarily, every pair of opposite faces is equal. Together with Step 2, this proves that the opposite faces of the solid are equal and parallelogrammic.
statement: If a solid be contained by parallel planes, the opposite planes in it are equal and parallelogrammic.

proof:
**Step 1.** Label the opposite faces of the given parallelepiped ABCD and A′B′C′D′, with corresponding vertices joined. Let the cutting plane be parallel to ADD′A′ and BCC′B′, meeting AB, DC, A′B′, D′C′ at E, F, E′, F′ respectively. Denote the base parallelograms AEFD and EBCF by B₁ and B₂, and the solids standing on them by S₁ and S₂. The sections are parallel to the corresponding face edges, and the two portions have parallelogrammic faces, by 11.16 and 11.24. We must prove B₁:B₂ = S₁:S₂.

**Step 2.** Path choice: use the equimultiple criterion D5.5 directly, constructing arbitrary equimultiples of both bases and solids within the same four lateral planes. Let m and n be arbitrary positive integers. Produce AB, DC, A′B′, D′C′ as necessary (P2). Starting at A on the ray AB, lay off m consecutive segments each equal to AE, ending at M; separately, starting again at A, lay off n consecutive segments each equal to EB, ending at N (1.3). Through every division point X draw, in the planes ABCD and ABB′A′, lines parallel to AD and AA′ respectively (1.31). These intersecting lines lie in a plane by 11.2, and that plane is parallel to ADD′A′ by 11.15. Use these planes as sections of the continued solid. Let U and V be the whole solids from ADD′A′ to the sections through M and N, and let R and T be their respective bases in the plane ABCD.

**Step 3.** Each newly bounded portion is contained by three pairs of parallel planes, so its faces are parallelograms (11.24). The edges of its transverse sections are parallel to the corresponding edges of ADD′A′ (11.16). Applying 1.34 to the lateral parallelograms between the initial section and any new section shows that every transverse edge has the corresponding fixed length AD or AA′. Applying 1.34 within each cell shows that its four longitudinal edges have the length of its segment on AB. Consequently, every cell in the first subdivision has corresponding edge lengths equal to those of S₁, and every cell in the second has corresponding edge lengths equal to those of S₂ (CN1).

**Step 4.** Compare a cell with its corresponding original solid S₁ or S₂. Corresponding lateral faces are parallelograms on equal bases and between the same parallel longitudinal lines; therefore they are equal by 1.36. This equality theorem is sufficient here because the bases being compared are equal. Corresponding end faces are equal by 11.24 applied to the portion between their section planes, or by CN4 when they coincide. Corresponding face angles are equal by 1.29 for faces in the same lateral plane and by 11.10 for end faces in distinct parallel planes. Together with Step 3, these angle and side equalities make the corresponding faces similar (D6.1). Thus the six corresponding faces are equal and similar, and the cell and its original solid are equal by D11.10. Their corresponding bases are equal as well. Hence the first subdivision consists of m cells equal to S₁ with bases equal to B₁, and the second of n cells equal to S₂ with bases equal to B₂.

**Step 5.** Adding these equal cells and their equal bases gives
R = mB₁,  U = mS₁,  T = nB₂,  V = nS₂,
where each multiple denotes repeated addition (CN2; D5.2). Thus R and U are corresponding equimultiples of B₁ and S₁, while T and V are corresponding equimultiples of B₂ and S₂.

**Step 6.** Both rows begin at the same end face and occupy the same four lateral planes. If M lies farther along the ray AB than N, then R contains T as a proper part, and U contains V as a proper part; hence R > T and U > V (CN5). If M and N coincide, the bases coincide and the solids coincide, so R = T and U = V (CN4). If M lies nearer A than N, the containments are reversed, so R < T and U < V (CN5). These cases exhaust the possible positions of M and N.

**Step 7.** Therefore, for every choice of positive integers m and n, mB₁ and nB₂ have exactly the same comparison as mS₁ and nS₂. By D5.5, B₁:B₂ = S₁:S₂. Thus, as the base is to the base, so is the solid to the solid.
statement: If a parallelepipedal solid be cut by a plane which is parallel to the opposite planes, then, as the base is to the base, so will the solid be to the solid.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given point on the given straight line l. Write the bounding rays of the given solid angle as OU₁, OU₂, …, OUₘ. Choose the numbering so that OU₁ and OU₂ are not collinear and U₃ lies outside their plane Π; this is possible because the given angle is solid. Choose a plane Σ through l and choose one ray of l issuing from A. The required solid angle will have this ray as a bounding edge. [D11.11, P1, 11.2]

**Step 2.** On the chosen ray mark B₁ so that AB₁ = OU₁. In Σ construct the ray AB₂ so that ∠B₁AB₂ = ∠U₁OU₂, and mark B₂ so that AB₂ = OU₂. Extend the rays first if necessary. The triangles AB₁B₂ and OU₁U₂ are congruent by side-angle-side. Our construction will copy this planar frame and then restore perpendicular heights; thus the prescribed edge remains fixed throughout. Side-angle-side is the natural criterion here because precisely two sides and their included angle have been copied. [P2, 1.3, 1.23, 1.4]

**Step 3.** For each Uᵢ outside Π, draw UᵢHᵢ perpendicular to Π, with Hᵢ in Π. For each Uᵢ already in Π, put Hᵢ = Uᵢ. In particular, H₁ = U₁ and H₂ = U₂, while U₃H₃ is a nonzero perpendicular height. [11.11]

**Step 4.** Copy every Hᵢ into Σ as a point Kᵢ as follows. If Hᵢ is not on the straight line OU₁, construct ∠B₁AKᵢ = ∠U₁OHᵢ and take AKᵢ = OHᵢ. Choose Kᵢ on the same side of AB₁ as B₂ exactly when Hᵢ is on the same side of OU₁ as U₂. If Hᵢ lies on the straight line OU₁ but differs from O, mark the equal distance on the corresponding forward or opposite ray of l. If Hᵢ = O, put Kᵢ = A. Thus K₁ = B₁ and K₂ = B₂. [1.23, 1.3, P2]

**Step 5.** These constructions give one congruent copy of the entire planar configuration of the feet. Indeed, superpose the congruent base triangles AB₁B₂ and OU₁U₂, matching A with O and B₁, B₂ with U₁, U₂. Each ray AKᵢ then coincides with OHᵢ: on a specified side of a baseline, two distinct rays cannot make the same angle with that baseline, since one such angle would be a proper part of the other. The equal distances AKᵢ = OHᵢ consequently make their endpoints coincide. The points on the baseline coincide for the same reason applied to lengths. This also covers feet outside the original face angle. [1.4, CN5]

**Step 6.** Fix corresponding sides of Π and Σ in this planar comparison. Whenever Uᵢ lies outside Π, erect at Kᵢ a perpendicular to Σ and mark on it a point Vᵢ such that KᵢVᵢ = HᵢUᵢ, choosing the side corresponding to the side of Π containing Uᵢ. Whenever Uᵢ lies in Π, put Vᵢ = Kᵢ. In particular, V₁ = B₁ and V₂ = B₂. All these operations are constructions of perpendiculars and copies of given lengths. [11.12, P2, 1.3]

**Step 7.** Join A to every Vᵢ. The rays AV₁ and AV₂ are distinct rays in Σ, while V₃ lies outside Σ because its perpendicular height is nonzero. No other plane can contain both AV₁ and AV₂: otherwise its intersection with Σ would contain two intersecting straight lines, whereas the intersection of distinct planes is a straight line. Thus the constructed rays are not all coplanar and constitute a solid angle at A, with AV₁ on the prescribed line l. [P1, 11.12, 11.3, D11.11]

**Step 8.** To verify equality, use the planar superposition established in Step 5, with the chosen sides corresponding. Every Kᵢ then coincides with Hᵢ. For each lifted point, the perpendicular rays KᵢVᵢ and HᵢUᵢ coincide, since two perpendiculars to the same plane cannot issue from the same point on the same side. Their equal lengths therefore make Vᵢ coincide with Uᵢ. The points lying in the base planes already coincide. Consequently every constructed bounding ray AVᵢ coincides with its corresponding original ray OUᵢ, and the whole solid angles coincide and are equal. Hence, on the given straight line and at its given point, a solid angle equal to the given solid angle has been constructed. [11.13, CN5, CN4, D11.11]
statement: On a given straight line, and at a given point on it, to construct a solid angle equal to a given solid angle.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line, and let OP, OQ, OR be the three edges meeting at a vertex O of the given parallelepiped. By 11.26 construct at A, on AB, a solid angle equal to the solid angle at O, with AB corresponding to OP and its other two rays corresponding respectively to OQ and OR. Thus the three corresponding plane angles are equal. This is the direct construction available here, since the whole solid angle is given; it need not be reconstructed from its separate plane angles.

**Step 2.** By 6.12 construct lengths c and d such that
OP : AB = OQ : c, and OP : AB = OR : d.
On the two remaining rays of the copied solid angle mark C and D so that AC = c and AD = d, producing the rays and cutting off the required lengths as necessary (P2, 1.3). Consequently
OP : AB = OQ : AC = OR : AD,
where the equality of the last two ratios follows from 5.11. Moreover, by the construction in Step 1,
∠BAC = ∠POQ, ∠BAD = ∠POR, and ∠CAD = ∠QOR.

**Step 3.** Complete the solid on the three edges AB, AC, AD as follows. Through B draw, in the planes ABC and ABD, straight lines parallel respectively to AC and AD (1.31). These intersecting lines determine a plane (11.2), which is parallel to ACD by 11.15. Similarly construct through C a plane parallel to ABD, and through D a plane parallel to ABC. These three planes, together with ABC, ABD, ACD, enclose a parallelepiped S having AB, AC, AD as its edges at A. Its opposite faces are equal and parallelogrammic by 11.24.

**Step 4.** Compare the three faces of S through A with the corresponding three faces of the given solid through O. All are parallelograms (11.24). In each corresponding pair, the angles at A and O are equal by Step 1. The remaining angles therefore agree also: adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary, and opposite angles are equal (1.29, 1.34). Their corresponding sides are proportional by Step 2, since opposite sides of each parallelogram are equal (1.34). Hence each of these three pairs of faces consists of similar rectilineal figures (D6.1).

**Step 5.** In either solid, the sides of a face opposite one of these three faces are respectively parallel and equal to the corresponding sides of that face: the intervening faces are parallelograms, whose opposite sides are parallel and equal (11.24, 1.34). The corresponding angles of these opposite faces are therefore equal to those of the faces already considered, by 11.10. Thus the remaining three pairs of faces inherit the equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides established in Step 4. They too are similar (D6.1).

**Step 6.** The two solids are consequently contained by six respectively similar faces, and are therefore similar solid figures (D11.9). They are also similarly situated: AB, AC, AD correspond in order to OP, OQ, OR in the equal solid angles constructed by 11.26, and the parallel-plane completion of Step 3 preserves this correspondence for the incident and opposite faces. Thus on the given straight line AB a parallelepipedal solid similar and similarly situated to the given parallelepipedal solid has been described.
statement: On a given straight line to describe a parallelepipedal solid similar and similarly situated to a given parallelepipedal solid.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the opposite faces of the parallelepiped be ABCD and EFGH, with joining edges AE, BF, CG, DH. Let the cutting plane pass through the diagonals AC and EG. By 11.24, all six faces are parallelograms, and opposite faces are equal. We shall use the direct boundary-face criterion of D11.10: compare the faces bounding the two parts.

**Step 2.** Since A and E lie in the cutting plane, the edge AE lies in it; similarly CG lies in it (11.1). The intersections of the cutting plane with the original faces are straight lines (11.3), so the section is the quadrilateral ACGE. The two parts therefore have the following boundary faces:
• first part: ABC, EFG, ABFE, BCGF, ACGE;
• second part: CDA, GHE, DCGH, ADHE, ACGE.
Here each diagonal divides its parallelogram face into the two indicated triangles (1.34).

**Step 3.** In parallelogram ABCD, the triangles ABC and CDA are equal, since its diagonal bisects it; moreover AB = CD and BC = DA (1.34). Their third side AC is common (CN4). Thus their corresponding angles are equal by 1.8, and, since their corresponding sides are equal and therefore proportional, they are also similar (D6.1). The same argument in parallelogram EFGH shows that triangles EFG and GHE are equal and similar (1.34, 1.8, D6.1).

**Step 4.** The faces ABFE and DCGH are opposite faces, as are BCGF and ADHE; hence each pair is equal (11.24). In each pair, corresponding sides are equal and parallel, being opposite sides of the adjoining parallelogram faces (1.34). Their corresponding angles are consequently equal by 11.10. Thus each pair consists of similar figures as well, since corresponding sides are equal and therefore proportional (D6.1).

**Step 5.** Finally, ACGE is the same face in both boundaries, so it is equal and similar to itself (CN4, D6.1). Consequently the two parts are bounded by five faces apiece, paired as equal and similar figures by Steps 3–4 and this common face. The two solids are therefore equal by D11.10. Since they are precisely the two parts into which the given plane cuts the parallelepiped, that plane bisects the solid.
statement: If a parallelepipedal solid be cut by a plane through the diagonals of the opposite planes, the solid will be bisected by the plane.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the two solids be S = ABCD–EFGH and T = ABCD–KLMN, with common base ABCD and standing edges AE, BF, CG, DH and AK, BL, CM, DN respectively. Label the vertices so that E, F, K, L lie on one straight line ℓ, and H, G, N, M on another straight line m, as the hypothesis permits. All their faces are parallelograms, and opposite faces are equal (11.24); their opposite edges are equal and parallel (1.34). Thus ℓ and m are parallel. The top vertices are coplanar; likewise A, B, E, F, K, L are coplanar, and D, C, H, G, N, M are coplanar (11.7).

**Step 2.** The joining edges EH, FG, KN, LM are equal and parallel, each being equal and parallel to AD (1.34, 11.9). If E = K, the corresponding upper vertices therefore coincide, and S = T by CN4. Otherwise, interchange the names of the solids if necessary so that K lies beyond E in the direction from E to F. Since EF = KL, the points E, F, L and E, K, L occur in these respective orders. Subtracting EF = KL from the common segment EL gives EK = FL (CN3). The corresponding orders on m are H, G, M and H, N, M; subtracting HG = NM from HM similarly gives HN = GM (1.34, CN3). No assumption is made about whether F precedes or follows K.

**Step 3.** Join E to L and H to M (P1), and consider the enclosing solid R bounded by the faces ABCD, ELMH, ABLE, DCMH, ADHE, and BCML. Its boundary gives two dissections (D11.2). Cutting along BCGF leaves S and the end-solid V whose triangular faces are BFL and CGM. Cutting along ADNK leaves T and the end-solid U whose triangular faces are AEK and DHN. Indeed, on the front face, BF divides ABLE into ABFE and BFL, while AK divides it into ABLK and AEK; the corresponding divisions occur on the opposite face. Thus R consists of S together with V, and also of T together with U, with disjoint interiors in each dissection. We use this common enclosure so that overlapping and nonoverlapping positions of the two upper faces require no separate cases.

**Step 4.** The triangular faces AEK and BFL are equal and similar: AE = BF and AK = BL by 1.34, while EK = FL by Step 2, so 1.8 applies. Likewise, DH = CG, DN = CM, and HN = GM, so DHN and CGM are equal and similar by 1.8 and D6.1. Side–side–side is the direct congruence criterion here because all three corresponding side equalities are already available.

**Step 5.** Two pairs of the remaining faces of U and V are
AEHD and BFGC, and AKND and BLMC.
The first pair consists of opposite faces of S, and the second of opposite faces of T; hence each pair is equal (11.24). Their corresponding sides are equal by 1.34, and their corresponding angles are equal because the sides containing them are respectively parallel (11.10). Therefore these face pairs are also similar (D6.1).

**Step 6.** The last faces are EKNH and FLMG. They are parallelograms: EK and HN lie on the parallel lines ℓ and m, as do FL and GM, while EH ∥ KN and FG ∥ LM by Step 2. Their bases EK and FL are equal, and they lie between the same parallels ℓ and m. Consequently they are equal by 1.36, which applies directly to these equal, though not necessarily identical, bases. Moreover, EH = FG by 1.34, their other corresponding sides are equal by 1.34 and Step 2, and their corresponding angles are equal by 1.29. Hence they are similar as well (D6.1).

**Step 7.** The five boundary faces of U are therefore respectively equal and similar to the five boundary faces of V, with the correspondence A ↔ B, E ↔ F, K ↔ L, D ↔ C, H ↔ G, N ↔ M. Thus U and V are equal and similar solids (D11.10), and in particular U = V.

**Step 8.** From the same enclosing solid R, subtract the equal end-solids U and V. The respective remainders are T and S by Step 3; therefore T = S (CN3). Hence parallelepipedal solids on the same base and of the same height, whose standing edges terminate on the same straight lines, are equal to one another.
statement: Parallelepipedal solids which are on the same base and of the same height, and in which the extremities of the sides which stand up are on the same straight lines, are equal to one another.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the given parallelepipedal solids be S = ABCD–EFGH and T = ABCD–KLMN, with standing edges AE, BF, CG, DH and AK, BL, CM, DN, respectively. Their faces are parallelograms (11.24). Let α be the plane of their common base ABCD. Their opposite faces lie in a common plane β parallel to α: these faces are parallel to the base and, by the equal-height hypothesis, are at the same perpendicular distance above it (D6.4).

**Step 2.** We choose to construct one intermediate parallelepiped and apply 11.29 twice. This directly uses the preceding equality theorem rather than introducing a subdivision or a proportional comparison. The intersections of the side-face planes with the parallel planes α and β give EF ∥ AB, GH ∥ CD, KN ∥ AD, and LM ∥ BC (11.16). Since ABCD is a parallelogram, transitivity of parallels gives EF ∥ GH ∥ AB and KN ∥ LM ∥ AD (1.30; 11.9).

**Step 3.** Produce the upper edges as necessary and define
X = EF ∩ KN, Y = EF ∩ LM, Z = GH ∩ LM, and W = GH ∩ KN (P2).
These intersections exist. Indeed, all four lines lie in β; the first pair has the direction of AB and the second pair the direction of AD. Since AB and AD meet, transitivity of parallels shows that no line of the first pair can be parallel to, or coincide with, a line of the second pair (1.30; 11.9). Coplanar lines which are not parallel meet when sufficiently produced (D1.23). Thus XYZW is a parallelogram, its opposite sides lying on EF and GH, and on KN and LM.

**Step 4.** Form the solid U bounded by α and β, by the two side-face planes ABEF and DCGH of S, and by the two side-face planes ADNK and BCML of T. These six planes occur in three parallel pairs. Their traces on α bound ABCD, and their traces on β bound XYZW. Their remaining intersections are the straight standing edges AX, BY, CZ, and DW (11.3). Hence U is a parallelepipedal solid, with parallelogrammic faces (11.24), on the same base ABCD and of the same height as S and T, since it lies between α and β (D6.4).

**Step 5.** Compare S and U. They have the same base and height. The upper extremities E, F, X, Y lie on the same straight line EF, while G, H, Z, W lie on the same straight line GH. Consequently S = U by 11.29.

**Step 6.** Compare U and T. Again they have the same base and height. The upper extremities X, W, K, N lie on the same straight line KN, while Y, Z, L, M lie on the same straight line LM. Consequently U = T by 11.29.

**Step 7.** Since S and T are equal to the same intermediate solid U, they are equal to one another (CN1). Therefore parallelepipedal solids on the same base and of the same height are equal in the stated case.
statement: Parallelepipedal solids which are on the same base and of the same height, and in which the extremities of the sides which stand up are not on the same straight lines, are equal to one another.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let S and T be parallelepipedal solids on equal bases and of the same perpendicular height h. Their bases are parallelograms by 11.24; height is understood as in D6.4. We shall reduce the solids to rectangular parallelepipeds and then compare them by cuts to which 11.25 applies.

**Step 2.** On each original base construct a right parallelepiped of height h. For this, erect a perpendicular to the base at one vertex (11.12), mark off length h on it (P2, 1.3), and complete the solid by parallels (1.31). The lateral edges are equal by 1.34 and are all perpendicular to the base by 11.8; the opposite face planes are parallel by 11.15. Denote these right parallelepipeds by S₀ and T₀.

**Step 3.** Since S and S₀ have the same base and height, they are equal; likewise T and T₀ are equal. Here 11.29 applies when the upper extremities lie on the same straight lines, and 11.30 applies in the complementary case. Thus S = S₀ and T = T₀. This uses the earlier 11.29 whenever its additional alignment hypothesis holds.

**Step 4.** Consider the base ABCD of S₀, with vertices in cyclic order. Draw through A a perpendicular to AB, meeting DC produced if necessary at F; through B draw its parallel, meeting the same line at G (1.11, 1.31, P2). Since AB is parallel to DC, ABGF is a rectangle by 1.29. The parallelograms ABCD and ABGF have the same base AB and lie between the same parallels AB and DC; hence they are equal by 1.35. Keeping the perpendicular edge at A, construct the right parallelepiped X on ABGF of height h by the construction of Step 2.

**Step 5.** Write A₁, B₁, C₁, D₁ for the upper vertices of S₀, and F₁, G₁ for the upper vertices above F, G in X. Regard S₀ and X as standing on their common rectangular face ABB₁A₁. Their opposite faces lie in the same plane through DC and D₁C₁, which is parallel to the common face by 11.15; consequently their heights relative to that face are equal. Moreover, D, C, F, G lie on the same straight line, and D₁, C₁, F₁, G₁ lie on the same straight line. Therefore S₀ = X by 11.29. Perform the same construction on T₀, obtaining a rectangular parallelepiped Y with T₀ = Y. By Step 4, 1.35, and CN1, the rectangular bases of X and Y are equal. Both solids still have height h.

**Step 6.** Let the adjacent sides of the rectangular base of X have lengths a, b, and those of the rectangular base of Y have lengths c, d. The rectangles are equiangular, since all right angles are equal (P4). Their equality therefore gives the reciprocal proportion

a : c = d : b

by 6.14.

**Step 7.** Construct a rectangular parallelepiped Z with perpendicular edge lengths c, b, h, using the construction of Step 2. Place X and Z together along their equal b-by-h faces, with their interiors on opposite sides; such placement does not change either solid (CN4). Their union is a rectangular parallelepiped, and the common face cuts it by a plane parallel to two opposite faces. Thus 11.25 gives

X : Z = (rectangle with sides a, b) : (rectangle with sides c, b).

These rectangles have the same height b, so 6.1 gives

X : Z = a : c.

**Step 8.** Similarly, place Y beside Z along their equal c-by-h faces (CN4). Their union is again a rectangular parallelepiped cut by the common face parallel to two opposite faces. By 11.25,

Y : Z = (rectangle with sides c, d) : (rectangle with sides c, b).

Taking d and b as the bases of these rectangles, their common height is c. Hence, by 6.1,

Y : Z = d : b.

**Step 9.** The proportion in Step 6 and the ratios in Steps 7–8 imply X : Z = Y : Z by 5.11. Magnitudes having the same ratio to the same magnitude are equal; therefore X = Y by 5.9.

**Step 10.** We have S = S₀ = X and T = T₀ = Y, while X = Y. Hence S = T by CN1. Therefore parallelepipedal solids on equal bases and of the same height are equal to one another.
statement: Parallelepipedal solids which are on equal bases and of the same height are equal to one another.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let S and T be parallelepipedal solids with respective bases P = ABCD and Q, and with the same height h. We shall construct, adjacent to S, a solid U whose base equals Q. The equal-base theorem 11.31 will then identify U with T in magnitude, while the single-cut theorem 11.25 will give the required ratio directly.

**Step 2.** Divide Q into two triangles by drawing a diagonal (P1). Produce AB beyond B and DC beyond C (P2). Apply the first triangle to BC as an equal parallelogram BGHC, outside ABCD, with BG along AB produced. Then apply the second triangle to GH as an equal parallelogram GEFH, beyond the first, with GE along BG produced (1.44, applied twice). Thus B, G, E are collinear, C, H, F are collinear, and BC, GH, EF are parallel. Consequently their union R = BEFC is a parallelogram, and AEFD is also a parallelogram (1.30). Since the two applied parallelograms equal the two triangles constituting Q, R = Q (CN2).

**Step 3.** Extend S in the direction AB to a parallelepiped W on the enlarged base AEFD, keeping its upper face in the plane of the original upper face. Explicitly, extend the corresponding edges of the upper face and draw through E and F lines parallel to the original rising edges (P2, 1.31). The new end-face through EF is parallel to the original end-face through BC, since their two intersecting edge-directions are respectively parallel (11.15). Let U be the part of W on BEFC. The original side-face through BC separates W into S and U and is parallel to W's opposite end-faces. Moreover, S and U lie between the same lower and upper planes, so U has height h.

**Step 4.** Apply 11.25 to this division of W. Its two base portions are P and R, and its two solid portions are S and U. Therefore
P : R = S : U.

**Step 5.** Since R = Q and U and T have the same height h, the equal-base theorem gives U = T (11.31). Equal magnitudes may replace one another in these ratios (5.7), and ratios equal to the same ratio are equal (5.11). Hence
S : T = P : Q.
Therefore parallelepipedal solids of the same height are to one another as their bases.
statement: Parallelepipedal solids which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let S and T be similar parallelepipedal solids. Let OA, OB, OC be the three edges of S issuing from one vertex, and let a, b, c denote the lengths of the corresponding edges of T. Their corresponding faces are similar, so
OA : a = OB : b = OC : c.
This follows by applying the proportionality of corresponding sides to the faces meeting at the chosen vertices. (D11.9, D6.1, 5.11.)

**Step 2.** On the ray OA, produced if necessary, take OX = a. (P2, 1.3.) Apply 11.27 on OX, using the already given solid angle of S at O, to construct a parallelepiped Q similar and similarly situated to S. Its other edges at O lie along the rays OB and OC; call them OY and OZ. Thus
OA : OX = OB : OY = OC : OZ.
Since OX = a, comparison with Step 1 gives OB : OY = OB : b and OC : OZ = OC : c. Consequently OY = b and OZ = c. (11.27, D6.1, 5.11, 5.9.)

**Step 3.** Corresponding faces of Q and T are similar, since each is similar to the corresponding face of S. (6.21.) For the three pairs of faces meeting at the chosen vertices, corresponding sides are equal by Step 2. These faces are therefore equal: by 6.20 their ratio is the duplicate ratio of equal sides, which is the ratio of equality. (6.20, D5.9, 5.9.) The other three pairs of faces are also equal, since opposite faces of each parallelepiped are equal. (11.24, CN1.) Hence Q and T are equal and similar solids; in particular, Q = T. (D11.10.)

**Step 4.** Complete two intermediate parallelepipeds: U with edges OX, OB, OC at O, and V with edges OX, OY, OC at O. The necessary parallels can be drawn by 1.31, and the opposite face planes are parallel by 11.15. Write [R,W] for the parallelogram with adjacent sides OR and OW. Our path is to change one edge at a time: each successive pair will have the same height, so 11.32 applies directly.

**Step 5.** Regard S and U as standing on the bases [A,B] and [X,B] in the plane OAB. Their opposite faces lie in the same parallel plane through C, so their heights are equal. (D6.4.) Therefore
S : U = [A,B] : [X,B]. (11.32.)
The two base parallelograms themselves have equal heights when OA and OX are taken as their bases: their opposite sides lie on the same parallel through B. Hence
[A,B] : [X,B] = OA : OX,
and consequently S : U = OA : OX. (6.1, 5.11.)

**Step 6.** Similarly, U and V stand on [X,B] and [X,Y] in the plane OAB, with their opposite faces in the same parallel plane through C. They therefore have equal heights. Their base parallelograms have equal heights when OB and OY are taken as bases, since their opposite sides lie on the same parallel through X. Thus
U : V = [X,B] : [X,Y] = OB : OY.
(D6.4, 11.32, 6.1, 5.11.)

**Step 7.** Now regard V and Q as standing on [Y,C] and [Y,Z] in the plane OBC. Their opposite faces lie in the same parallel plane through X, so these solids also have equal heights. The two base parallelograms have equal heights when OC and OZ are taken as bases, since their opposite sides lie on the same parallel through Y. Consequently
V : Q = [Y,C] : [Y,Z] = OC : OZ.
(D6.4, 11.32, 6.1, 5.11.)

**Step 8.** Combining Steps 2 and 5–7 gives
S : U = U : V = V : Q = OA : OX. (5.11.)
Thus S, U, V, Q are four continuously proportional magnitudes. By the definition of triplicate ratio, S : Q is the triplicate ratio of OA : OX. (D5.10.) Since Q = T and OX = a, substitution of equals gives that S : T is the triplicate ratio of OA : a. (5.7.) The chosen edges were corresponding edges of the given solids. Therefore similar parallelepipedal solids are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides.
statement: Similar parallelepipedal solids are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let S and T be parallelepipedal solids with bases A and B and perpendicular heights h and k, respectively. We must prove that S = T if and only if A : B = k : h. Construct a rectangle R equal in area to B, using 1.45 with a right angle, and denote its adjacent side lengths by u and v. [1.45]

**Step 2.** On R construct rectangular parallelepipeds U and V of heights h and k, respectively. For this, erect a perpendicular to the plane of R at a vertex, produce it as necessary, mark off the prescribed heights, and complete the solids by parallels. The edges parallel to the erected perpendicular are also perpendicular to the base plane, and the opposite face planes are parallel. [11.12, P2, 1.3, 1.31, 11.8, 11.15]

**Step 3.** Since T and V have equal bases B and R and the same height k, they are equal: T = V. [11.31] Path choice: use the equal-base, equal-height theorem for this replacement, and then use the equal-height ratio theorem for the comparisons below. The rectangular construction allows side faces to serve as bases, converting the comparison of heights into a comparison of areas.

**Step 4.** The solids S and U have the same height h. Therefore their ratio is the ratio of their bases. Since R = B,
S : U = A : R = A : B. [11.32, 5.7]

**Step 5.** Let Fₖ and Fₕ be the rectangular side faces of V and U erected on the same side of R of length u. Viewed as parallelograms with bases of lengths k and h, these faces have the same height u. Hence
Fₖ : Fₕ = k : h. [6.1]
Now regard Fₖ and Fₕ as the bases of V and U. In each solid the edge of length v is perpendicular to the two intersecting edge directions in the chosen base, and therefore perpendicular to its plane. Thus both solids have height v relative to these bases. [11.4] Applying the equal-height ratio theorem gives
V : U = Fₖ : Fₕ = k : h. [11.32, 5.11]

**Step 6.** Suppose first that S = T. Since T = V by Step 3, S = V. [CN1] Equal magnitudes have the same ratio to U, so S : U = V : U. [5.7] Combining this equality with Steps 4 and 5 yields
A : B = k : h.
Thus equal parallelepipedal solids have their bases reciprocally proportional to their heights. [5.11]
