**Step 7.** Conversely, suppose that A : B = k : h. Steps 4 and 5 then give S : U = V : U. [5.11] Magnitudes having the same ratio to the same magnitude are equal, so S = V. [5.9] Since V = T by Step 3, S = T. [CN1] Therefore parallelepipedal solids whose bases are reciprocally proportional to their heights are equal, completing both directions.
statement: In equal parallelepipedal solids the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those parallelepipedal solids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the equal plane angles have vertices A and A′ and lie in planes π and π′, with their side-rays correspondingly paired. Let P and R be the given points on the elevated rays, and let PH and RK be their perpendiculars to π and π′. Join AH and A′K, the joining lines specified in the statement. These joins lie in their respective planes. We must prove ∠PAH = ∠RA′K. Every triangle used below is planar. [Hypotheses; P1; D1.7; 11.2]

**Step 2.** First normalize the lengths of the elevated segments. Interchanging the configurations if necessary, suppose AP ≤ A′R. Take Q on A′R with A′Q = AP. If Q = R, put L = K; otherwise, in triangle A′RK draw through Q the parallel to RK, meeting the side A′K at L. Then QL is perpendicular to π′. Moreover, A′Q and A′R are the same ray, as are A′L and A′K, so ∠QA′L = ∠RA′K. It therefore suffices to prove ∠PAH = ∠QA′L. [1.3; 1.31; 11.8]

**Step 3.** Draw in π a transversal through H which does not pass through A and is not parallel to either original side-line. Let it meet those complete side-lines at B and C. On the corresponding complete side-lines in π′ take B′ and C′ with A′B′ = AB and A′C′ = AC. Choose each corresponding pair of rays simultaneously in the original directions or simultaneously in the opposite directions. [P1; P2; 1.3]

Reversing one side-ray replaces an affected angle by its supplement; reversing both sides of a plane angle preserves it as a vertically opposite angle. Consequently, the hypotheses give
∠BAC = ∠B′A′C′,
∠PAB = ∠QA′B′,
and ∠PAC = ∠QA′C′,
regardless of which extensions contain B and C. [1.13; 1.15; P4; CN3]

**Step 4.** Apply side-angle-side equality to the respective pairs of triangles ABC and A′B′C′, APB and A′QB′, and APC and A′QC′. Their corresponding sides and angles are equal. In particular,
BC = B′C′, PB = QB′, and PC = QC′,
and ∠ABC = ∠A′B′C′. [1.4]

**Step 5.** Thus triangles PBC and QB′C′ have their three corresponding sides equal, so their corresponding angles are equal. In particular, ∠PBC = ∠QB′C′ and ∠PCB = ∠QC′B′. Side-side-side equality is the natural next criterion here because all three side equalities have already been obtained. [1.8]

**Step 6.** Suppose first that H is distinct from B and C. On the complete line B′C′ take X such that B′X = BH, choosing the ray B′X toward C′ exactly when the ray BH is toward C. [P2; 1.3]

The angles ∠ABH and ∠A′B′X are therefore equal, and so are ∠PBH and ∠QB′X. Indeed, these are either the corresponding equal angles at B and B′ obtained in Steps 4–5, or the supplements of those angles. This also covers H lying on an extension of BC. [1.13; P4; CN3]

**Step 7.** Triangles ABH and A′B′X have AB = A′B′, BH = B′X, and their included angles equal; hence AH = A′X. Likewise, triangles PBH and QB′X have PB = QB′, BH = B′X, and their included angles equal; hence PH = QX and ∠PHB = ∠QXB′. [1.4]

Since PH is perpendicular to π, ∠PHB is right. Therefore QX is perpendicular to XB′. [D11.3]

**Step 8.** The three corresponding sides of triangles APH and A′QX are now equal: AP = A′Q, AH = A′X, and PH = QX. Therefore
∠PAH = ∠QA′X and ∠PHA = ∠QXA′. [1.8]

The angle ∠PHA is right because PH is perpendicular to π. Thus QX is also perpendicular to XA′. The intersecting lines XA′ and XB′ are distinct and lie in π′, since A′ is not on B′C′. Consequently QX is perpendicular to π′. [D11.3; 11.4]

**Step 9.** If instead H = B, put X = B′. The equality of triangles APB and A′QB′ gives ∠PAH = ∠QA′X and makes QX perpendicular to XA′. The equality of the corresponding angles of triangles PBC and QB′C′ makes QX perpendicular to XC′, since PH is perpendicular to BC. Hence QX is perpendicular to π′. [1.4; 1.8; D11.3; 11.4]

If H = C, put X = C′ and use triangles APC and A′QC′, together with PBC and QB′C′, in exactly the same way: ∠PAH = ∠QA′X, and QX is perpendicular to both XA′ and XB′, hence to π′. [1.4; 1.8; D11.3; 11.4]

**Step 10.** In every case, QX is perpendicular to π′ and ∠PAH = ∠QA′X. But QL is also perpendicular to π′ by Step 2. If QX and QL were distinct lines, they would be parallel, although both pass through Q; this is impossible. They therefore coincide, and their intersections X and L with π′ are the same point. [11.6; D1.23; 11.1]

It follows that ∠PAH = ∠QA′L = ∠RA′K. Thus the straight lines joining the perpendicular feet to the original vertices contain equal angles with the elevated straight lines, as required. [CN1]
statement: If there be two equal plane angles, and on their vertices there be set up elevated straight lines containing equal angles with the original straight lines respectively, if on the elevated straight lines points be taken at random and perpendiculars be drawn from them to the planes in which the original angles are, and if from the points so arising in the planes straight lines be joined to the vertices of the original angles, they will contain, with the elevated straight lines, equal angles.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the three given lengths be a, b, c, with a:b = b:c, expressing their proportionality (D5.6). Let S be the parallelepiped with coinitial edges OA = a, OB = c, OC = b. Let T be the equilateral parallelepiped equiangular with S, with corresponding edges O′A′ = O′B′ = O′C′ = b. Choose the faces through OA, OB and O′A′, O′B′ as bases. This choice places the extreme lengths in the first base and leaves equal standing edges in the two solids.

**Step 2.** The chosen bases are equiangular by hypothesis, and
OA:O′A′ = O′B′:OB,
since a:b = b:c. Their sides about corresponding equal angles are therefore reciprocally proportional. Hence the two bases are equal by 6.14.

**Step 3.** Suppose first that either standing edge, OC or O′C′, is perpendicular to its base plane. Its angles with both base edges are then right (D11.3). By equiangularity, the corresponding angles in the other solid are also right; consequently its standing edge is likewise perpendicular to its base plane (11.4). In this case the heights are the standing edges themselves, both of length b, and are therefore equal.

**Step 4.** In the remaining case neither standing edge is perpendicular to its base. Draw CH and C′H′ perpendicular to the respective base planes (11.11), and join OH and O′H′ (P1). Here H differs from O and H′ differs from O′, since otherwise the corresponding standing edge would be perpendicular to its base. The base angles AOB and A′O′B′ are equal, and the elevated edges OC and O′C′ make equal angles with the corresponding base edges, by the assumed equiangularity. Therefore 11.35 gives
∠COH = ∠C′O′H′.

**Step 5.** The angles CHO and C′H′O′ are right by D11.3, and hence equal by P4. Thus triangles COH and C′O′H′ have two corresponding angles equal and the corresponding sides OC and O′C′, opposite their right angles, equal to b. By 1.26, CH = C′H′. These perpendiculars are the heights of the respective solids, so their heights are equal in this case also.

**Step 6.** The solids have equal bases by Step 2 and equal heights by Steps 3–5. The equal-base, equal-height criterion 11.31 therefore gives S = T. Hence the parallelepipedal solid formed from the three proportional straight lines is equal to the equilateral parallelepipedal solid on the mean which is equiangular with it.
statement: If three straight lines be proportional, the parallelepipedal solid formed out of the three is equal to the parallelepipedal solid on the mean which is equilateral, but equiangular with the aforesaid solid.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let a, b, c, d be the four straight lines, and let K, L, M, N respectively be the similar and similarly described parallelepipedal solids on them, with these lines as corresponding edges. We use 11.33 directly, since it gives precisely the relation between these solids and their corresponding edges. For the converse, we will construct a fourth proportional rather than assume that equality of triplicate ratios can be cancelled. [11.33]

**Step 2.** First suppose that a:b = c:d. By successive applications of 6.11, construct straight lines p, q, r, s such that
 a:b = b:p = p:q,
 c:d = d:r = r:s.
[6.11]

**Step 3.** The hypothesis and these constructions give equal corresponding successive ratios in the sequences a, b, p, q and c, d, r, s. Therefore, ex aequali,
 a:q = c:s.
[5.11, 5.22]

**Step 4.** By the definition of triplicate ratio and 11.33,
 K:L = a:q and M:N = c:s.
Consequently K:L = M:N. This proves the forward implication. [D5.10, 11.33, 5.11]

**Step 5.** Conversely, suppose that K:L = M:N. Construct a fourth proportional e to a, b, c, so that
 a:b = c:e.
On e describe a parallelepipedal solid T of the same prescribed similar form and corresponding situation as the given solids. [6.12, 11.27]

**Step 6.** The forward implication established in Steps 2–4 gives K:L = M:T. Together with the present hypothesis, this yields M:N = M:T. Magnitudes to which the same magnitude has the same ratio are equal; hence N = T. [5.11, 5.9]

**Step 7.** Construct straight lines u and v such that
 d:e = e:u = u:v.
Since N and T are similar solids on the corresponding edges d and e, their ratio is the triplicate ratio of d:e; thus
 N:T = d:v.
But N = T. Taking single copies of the four magnitudes in the definition of equal ratios therefore gives d = v. [6.11, D5.10, 11.33, D5.5]

**Step 8.** If d were greater than e, the proportion d:e = e:u would imply e > u, and the proportion e:u = u:v would then imply u > v. Thus d > e > u > v, contrary to d = v. If d were less than e, the same applications would give d < e < u < v, again contrary to d = v. Therefore d = e. [5.14]

**Step 9.** Since d = e, we have c:e = c:d. Combining this with a:b = c:e gives a:b = c:d. Thus the proportionality of the solids implies the proportionality of the straight lines, and both assertions are proved. [5.7, 5.11]
statement: If four straight lines be proportional, the parallelepipedal solids on them which are similar and similarly described will also be proportional; and, if the parallelepipedal solids on them which are similar and similarly described be proportional, the straight lines will themselves also be proportional.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCD and EFGH be the opposite square faces of the cube, with AE, BF, CG, DH joining corresponding vertices. Let K, L, M, N bisect AB, BC, CD, DA respectively, and let K′, L′, M′, N′ bisect EF, FG, GH, HE respectively. Denote the cutting planes through K, M, K′, M′ and through L, N, L′, N′ by π and σ. Join AC, EG, and the cube diameter AG. We shall work in the diagonal plane containing these lines, reducing the conclusion to a comparison of plane triangles. [D11.25, P1]

**Step 2.** The opposite sides of each square face are equal and parallel. Thus KB and MC are equal and parallel, and 1.33 gives KM ∥ BC. Likewise BL and AN are equal and parallel, so 1.33 gives LN ∥ AB. Here the equalities of the half-sides follow because halves of equal magnitudes are equal. The same argument applies to the upper face. [D1.22, 1.28, CN2, CN5, 1.33]

**Step 3.** Let KM meet AC at O. In triangle ABC, because KO ∥ BC, we have AK:KB = AO:OC. Since AK = KB, it follows that AO = OC. Similarly, in triangle CBA, the line LN, being parallel to BA and passing through the midpoint L of CB, meets CA at its midpoint. Consequently LN also passes through O, since a segment has only one midpoint. Applying the identical argument in EFGH, the lines K′M′ and L′N′ meet at a point O′ satisfying EO′ = O′G. [6.2, D5.5, CN5]

**Step 4.** The traces of π on the two opposite faces are KM and K′M′, while those of σ are LN and L′N′. Hence both cutting planes contain O and O′. Their common section is therefore the straight line OO′, whose portion within the cube is the segment between these opposite faces. [11.3]

**Step 5.** The square lateral faces give AE ∥ BF and BF ∥ CG; therefore AE ∥ CG. They also give AE = AB = BC = CG. The parallel edges AE and CG lie in one plane, and their joining lines AC and EG lie in that plane. Since AE and CG are equal and parallel, 1.33 gives AC ∥ EG and AC = EG. Thus ACGE is a parallelogram containing AG, O, and O′. [D1.22, 1.28, 11.9, CN1, 11.7, 1.33]

**Step 6.** In this parallelogram, O lies inside AC and O′ lies inside EG, on opposite sides of the diagonal AG. Hence OO′ meets AG at an interior point X. Since AO and GO′ are halves of the equal segments AC and EG, we have AO = GO′. Moreover, AC ∥ EG gives ∠OAX = ∠O′GX and ∠AOX = ∠GO′X, by alternate angles with the transversals AG and OO′ respectively. [Step 5, CN2, CN5, 1.29]

**Step 7.** The triangles AOX and GO′X therefore have two corresponding angles equal and the intervening sides AO and GO′ equal. By 1.26—the congruence criterion directly supplied by these parallel-line angle equalities—we obtain AX = XG and OX = XO′. Thus the diameter AG and the common section OO′ of the cutting planes bisect one another, as required. [1.26]
statement: If the sides of the opposite planes of a cube be bisected, and planes be carried through the points of section, the common section of the planes and the diameter of the cube bisect one another.

proof:
**Step 1.** Use the side-base convention for the first prism: its parallelogram base is a lateral face of a triangular-ended prism. Let this prism be P, with supporting base ABCD, triangular ends ABE and DCF, and opposite edge EF. Let the other prism Q have triangular base KLM and opposite triangular face K′L′M′. Their common height is h, and ABCD is double triangle KLM. The remaining faces of each prism are parallelograms. (Hypothesis; D11.13.)

**Step 2.** Complete ABE and DCF to parallelograms ABGE and DCHF by drawing the requisite parallels. This completes P to a parallelepiped R with base ABCD and opposite face EGHF. Since EG is parallel to AB and EF is parallel to AD, the plane EGHF is parallel to ABCD. It contains the opposite edge EF of P, so R has the same height h as P. (1.31; 11.15; D6.4.)

**Step 3.** The plane BCEF passes through BE and CF, which are diagonals of the opposite faces ABGE and DCHF of R. It therefore bisects R. One of its two parts is precisely P; hence R is double P. (11.28.)

**Step 4.** Similarly, complete KLM to the parallelogram KLNM, whose diagonal is LM, and complete K′L′M′ correspondingly to K′L′N′M′. These completions give a parallelepiped S containing Q. Its base and opposite face remain in the two original triangular-face planes, so its height is h. Moreover, the diagonal LM bisects KLNM; consequently KLNM is double triangle KLM. (1.31; D11.13; D6.4; 1.34.)

**Step 5.** The plane through LM and L′M′ passes through diagonals of the opposite faces KLNM and K′L′N′M′ of S. It therefore bisects S, and one of the resulting parts is Q. Thus S is double Q. (11.28.)

**Step 6.** By hypothesis ABCD is double triangle KLM, and by Step 4 so is KLNM. Hence the bases ABCD and KLNM are equal. The parallelepipeds R and S also have the same height h, so they are equal. This is the direct equal-base, equal-height route; no general proportionality theorem for solids is required. (CN1; 11.31.)

**Step 7.** Since R is double P and S is double Q, the ratios R:P and S:Q are equal: for any positive integers m and n, the comparison of mR with nP is determined by the comparison of 2m with n, exactly as is the comparison of mS with nQ. Since R=S, one and the same magnitude therefore has the same ratio to P and Q. It follows that P=Q. Thus the two prisms are equal. (D5.5; 5.9.)
statement: If there be two prisms of equal height, and one have a parallelogram as base and the other a triangle, and if the parallelogram be double of the triangle, the prisms will be equal.
